blocks.text: During a chemical reaction reactants are converted into products, so the concentration of the products rises as that of the reactants falls.

blocks.title: Rate of reaction
blocks.text: The rate of a reaction is the change in the concentration of a reactant or a product divided by the time taken for the change: rate = delta x / delta t, where delta x is a very small change in concentration in a very small time interval delta t.

For a reactant A changing irreversibly to a product B, the slope of the concentration-time graph is steepest at the beginning, showing a rapid fall in the reactant and a rapid rise in the product; as the reaction proceeds the slope becomes less steep, the reaction slows with time, and finally both curves become parallel at the completion of the reaction. So the rate of a reaction changes every moment. The units of rate are concentration divided by time, usually mol dm-3 s-1; for slow reactions mol dm-3 min-1 or mol dm-3 h-1 may be used, and for gas-phase reactions units of pressure replace molar concentration. For A giving B the rate can be written as the rate of disappearance of A or the rate of appearance of B: rate = -delta[A]/delta t = +delta[B]/delta t, the negative sign showing the decrease in the reactant's concentration and the positive sign the increase in the product's.

blocks.alt: Graph with axes O-Y (an upward arrow beside it) and O-X (Time). For A to B, the curve 'Concentration of reactant "A"' falls steeply from a high value at the start and flattens towards the time axis; the curve 'Concentration of product "B"' rises steeply from zero and flattens. Both curves carry plotted points and cross early in the reaction.
